﻿Ran into this same problem and did some exact measurements. Downloaded all 16 tool .txt files from `packages/opencode/src/tool/` and counted characters:

bash.txt is the worst offender at 9,288 chars (~2,654 tokens). What's wild is that 63% of it (5,874 chars / ~1,678 tokens) is git commit and PR creation instructions that have nothing to do with actually executing bash commands.

The key insight I found: tool descriptions are NOT cacheable, but system prompt text IS (Anthropic prompt caching, OpenAI cached prefix). Those git/PR instructions get paid for on every single API turn, even when the user never touches git.

Full breakdown:

- bash.txt: 9,288 chars — 63% git/PR instructions
- task.txt: 3,799 chars
- multiedit.txt: 2,406 chars
- edit.txt: 1,369 chars
- apply_patch.txt: 1,092 chars
- read.txt: 1,158 chars
- lsp.txt: 1,040 chars
- websearch.txt: 976 chars
- batch.txt: 998 chars
- codesearch.txt: 802 chars
- webfetch.txt: 750 chars
- question.txt: 657 chars
- grep.txt: 689 chars
- write.txt: 623 chars
- glob.txt: 545 chars
- ls.txt: 314 chars

Total: ~26,500 chars (~7,573 tokens) for built-in tool descriptions alone. In my setup (5 MCP servers + plugin), a fresh session hits ~40K tokens before the first user message.

I opened #21345 with a specific proposal to move the git/PR sections out of bash.txt and into the system prompt where they'd be cacheable. That alone would save ~1,678 tokens per request.

I want to add a more specific use case here because it matches what I am looking for very closely.

The capability I want is not just parent -> child context inheritance.
It is shared task-scoped context across parallel sibling subagents.

More concretely:
- several subagents are spawned under one parent task
- they should be able to see shared findings, constraints, decisions, and intermediate artifacts from each other
- ideally without copying full transcript history into every child session
- the parent should not be the only relay point for all coordination

Why this matters:
- avoids duplicate exploration across parallel agents
- lets one agent's discovery immediately inform another agent's work
- improves reviewer / implementer / researcher coordination
- makes multi-agent execution feel like one collaborative task rather than isolated branches that only report back upward

A shared scratchpad / shared memory bus / task-level coordination layer would solve the actual problem for me.

So if design choices need to be prioritized, my strongest request is:
first-class sibling-to-sibling shared context for agents working on the same task, not only parent-child session linkage.

I’m hitting the same underlying problem with an observer-style plugin.
My plugin watches the conversation and periodically curates `docs/knowledge/`. The problem is that the only practical way to trigger it is via `client.session.prompt()`, which is not truly background work: it injects a new turn into the active session.
What I need is:
1. a reliable “turn completed” signal only after all `session/update` notifications have been flushed and the `session/prompt` lifecycle is actually finished
2. the ability to run plugin-initiated follow-up work without interrupting or polluting the primary agent turn
3. ideally, a real background / fire-and-forget session mechanism, or a dedicated hook for post-turn async work
Right now, if a plugin tries to do observer/background orchestration, it either:
- fires too early
- interleaves with the active turn
- or sends updates that look stale / unsolicited from the ACP client’s perspective
So from my side this is not just an ACP client rendering issue; it also blocks a class of plugins that need “after-turn, non-intrusive” execution.
Questions:
- Would fixing the ordering in this issue also make plugin-triggered follow-up work safe?
- Is PR #21316 expected to cover plugin/background-triggered cases too?
- If not, should this be modeled as a separate feature: a post-`end_turn` hook or true background prompt API for plugins?

I agree with this issue. In most Make and CMake projects, Makefile and CMakeLists.txt do not indicate the project root — they exist in countless subdirectories throughout the tree.

**llvm-project** (https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project) is good example. llvm-project  has CMakeLists.txt in every single subdirectory like clang/lib/Sema/, clang/lib/AST/, clang/lib/CodeGen/, etc. Opening any file there causes clangd to start in the wrong directory.
These markers should be removed from the clangd root detection. Only compile_commands.json, compile_flags.txt, and .clangd reliably indicate where clangd should run.
